item.description: DEPUTY Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica asserts that The People’s Alliance party possesses a profound advantage over political rivals through its formidable depth of capable leaders rather than depending on a single figurehead. In an interview on The Fiji Times’ online portal The Lens@177, Mr Kamikamica said the party relied on collective capability, citing high-profile ministers and assistant mini
item.content:encoded:
DEPUTY Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica asserts that The People’s Alliance party possesses a profound advantage over political rivals through its formidable depth of capable leaders rather than depending on a single figurehead.

In an interview on The Fiji Times’ online portal The Lens@177, Mr Kamikamica said the party relied on collective capability, citing high-profile ministers and assistant ministers who command strong leadership credentials in their own right.

He said opposing political parties making a single individual the focal point of national leadership misunderstand how progress works.

Mr Kamikamica reiterated that sustainable national development required collective cooperation and shared objectives rather than solitary heroism.

He emphasised that the party’s foundation of shared experience and genuine public service commitment differentiated them from alternative political movements.

item.title: HIV cases up among teenagers – Ravunawa
item.description: FIJI is seeing an increase in HIV diagnosis among young people, with those aged 10 to 19 accounting for a growing proportion of cases. The Assistant Health Minister Penioni Ravunawa says HIV infections among children and teenagers aged 10 to 19 had increased by 45 per cent.
item.content:encoded:
FIJI is seeing an increase in HIV diagnosis among young people, with those aged 10 to 19 accounting for a growing proportion of cases.

The Assistant Health Minister Penioni Ravunawa says HIV infections among children and teenagers aged 10 to 19 had increased by 45 per cent.

“This is of particular concern to us today because of the impact on young people,” he said.

Mr Ravunawa said the increase was a warning that young people needed to receive the right information about HIV and sexual health.

“We have also seen a 45 per cent increase in infections among children and teenagers aged 10 to 19 years.”

He said parents, families, schools and communities had an important role in protecting children.

“Young people needed to understand how HIV was spread and how they could protect themselves.

“Know the facts. Know your status. Protect your future.”

He urged young people not to feel ashamed about getting tested.

Fiji recorded 2016 new HIV diagnoses in 2025, compared to 245 in 2022.

item.title: ‘Confront social ills’
item.description: Head of the Catholic Church Archbishop Peter Loy Chong has challenged Fiji’s churches to stop measuring their success by church numbers and baptisms and instead confront the social crises affecting the country, including drugs, violence, HIV and the growing impact of social media on children. Speaking during the service in Lakeba, Lau, to commemorate 182 years since the arrival of the first Cathol
item.content:encoded:
Head of the Catholic Church Archbishop Peter Loy Chong has challenged Fiji’s churches to stop measuring their success by church numbers and baptisms and instead confront the social crises affecting the country, including drugs, violence, HIV and the growing impact of social media on children.

Speaking during the service in Lakeba, Lau, to commemorate 182 years since the arrival of the first Catholic missionaries in Fiji, Archbishop Loy Chong said Christian mission should not be about competing for members, but about bringing meaningful change to people’s lives.

“Christian mission cannot simply be about tallying baptisms or switching people from one church roster to another,” he said.

He said the focus should instead be on “a deep transformation of attitude”, including rejecting violence, respecting women, protecting children, upholding honesty in leadership and caring for creation.

Archbishop Loy Chong said the church needed to examine whether its work was addressing the challenges people faced in their everyday lives.

“The urgent question before us today is this: How are we practising our faith in God so that it speaks directly and healingly to the deep social challenges of our people?”

He highlighted what he described as the “devastating scourge” of illicit drugs, including methamphetamine and marijuana, and their impact on young people.

Archbishop Loy Chong also raised concern about the growing influence of technology on children.

“We see our children consumed and alienated by smartphones, social media, and digital addiction.”

He said the church could not remain focused solely on what happened inside places of worship while communities struggled with serious social problems.

“The world is hurting outside the doors of our churches. If our religion remains locked inside our four walls, what good is it?”

Archbishop Loy Chong said churches needed to respond through practical action and work together to address the challenges facing communities.

He said Christian mission should bring about a change in attitudes and behaviour, rather than simply increasing church membership.

He called for greater cooperation between churches, saying the challenges facing communities required a united response.

“The era of religious competition is behind us – the era of united Christian witness is here.”

item.title: Council activates measures as dry spell persists
item.description: FOOD security, water supply and animal feed are among the concerns that cane farmers will have to contend with aside from harvesting cane during the prolonged dry period. Sugar Cane Growers Council CEO Vimal Dutt said the industry has activated immediate measures to address these concerns.
item.content:encoded:
FOOD security, water supply and animal feed are among the concerns that cane farmers will have to contend with aside from harvesting cane during the prolonged dry period.

Sugar Cane Growers Council CEO Vimal Dutt said the industry has activated immediate measures to address these concerns.

“We had a meeting with our industry stakeholders, and a few immediate concerns were raised during the meeting which we will have to address.

“These include food security, water supply and animal feed for the grower’s livestock,” said Mr Dutt.

“This is apart from the concerns about the cane harvesting.

“So we are putting in immediate measures and the first being sending out advisories to our growers to actively preserve water supply and animal feed for their livestock.”

He said growers would also be discouraged from planting ratoons during the dry spell.

“For the time being we are also asking our growers to not plant ratoons at the moment.

“Once the weather improves then they would be encouraged to plant them.

“One of the issues we will work with the Sugar Research Institute is the supply of seed cane which they will need to supply to our growers and ensure that supply is maintained and sufficient.”

The prolonged dry spell is fuelled by an El Nino which brings below normal rainfall to Fiji is currently present in the tropical Pacific Ocean.

According to the Fiji Meteorological Services, both ocean and atmospheric conditions are showing stronger El Niño signals, indicating that the event is likely to continue strengthening until next year.

Most global climate models suggest that this El Niño event is likely to reach strong to very strong intensity and persist through the end of 2026 and into early 2027.

item.title: Koroi to advocate for mental health
item.description: LOSING her father at a young age and experiencing the challenges that followed taught Miss Grace Road Keren Koroi that there is always hope, regardless of the circumstances. The 21-year-old, who hails from Tuvuca Island in Vanuabalavu, Lau, with maternal links to Lomaiviti, is a final-year land surveying student at Fiji National University.
item.content:encoded:
LOSING her father at a young age and experiencing the challenges that followed taught Miss Grace Road Keren Koroi that there is always hope, regardless of the circumstances.

The 21-year-old, who hails from Tuvuca Island in Vanuabalavu, Lau, with maternal links to Lomaiviti, is a final-year land surveying student at Fiji National University.

Ms Koroi said her experiences, including her mother’s journey through widowhood, raising three kids alone and later remarriage, shaped her decision to advocate for hope through mental health awareness.

“That is exactly why I am advocating for hope through mental health awareness, because I believe that a healthy mind is a healthier you,” she said.

Ms Koroi said she entered the Miss Hibiscus contest to overcome her fear of being seen and use her voice to encourage others to face their own fears.

“I entered it because I want to face that fear.”

She said she had also experienced anxiety, suicidal thoughts and other mental health struggles while in high school.

Ms Koroi said motivational speakers helped her during that period, with advice from Steve Harvey also influencing her decision to pursue land surveying.

She said she chose the field because she loved drawing, mathematics and the outdoors.

Ms Koroi encouraged young women who were undecided about their future to pursue their interests.

“Go for it. What are you waiting for? There’s nothing to be afraid of.”

She said the biggest obstacle could be a person’s own mind and encouraged young people to believe in themselves.

item.title: El Niño hits sugar sector
item.description: SUGARcane production is expected to drop by about 200,000 tonnes this season, with El Niño contributing to the decline, says incoming Sugar Minister Charan Jeath Singh. Mr Singh said the industry had initially forecast a cane production of about 1.5 million tonnes for this season.
item.content:encoded:
SUGARcane production is expected to drop by about 200,000 tonnes this season, with El Niño contributing to the decline, says incoming Sugar Minister Charan Jeath Singh.

Mr Singh said the industry had initially forecast a cane production of about 1.5 million tonnes for this season.

However, that estimate had now fallen to about 1.3 million tonnes.

“I was told that even in this current season, whilst we were forecasting about 1.5 million tonnes of cane, because of the El Niño effect, there is a drop in the sugar tonnage itself from 1.5 to 1.3 million,” he said.

He said the decline was also being reflected in Labasa, where production had been forecast at about 650,000 tonnes.

He said the estimate had now dropped to about 550,000 tonnes.

“The sugar mills needs sufficient cane supply to operate effectively.”

He identified the decline in cane production as one of several major challenges facing the sugar industry.

“Ageing machinery, problems faced by farmers and the declining number of young people entering cane farming were also affecting the industry.

He said expiring land leases as another concern, adding that farmers needed certainty over the future of their land if they were to remain in the industry.

item.title: Kamikamica backs MPs
item.description: THERE are capable leaders within the Peoples Alliance party, says Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica. In an interview on The Fiji Times online portal The Lens@177, Mr Kamikamica said this was one of the party’s strengths compared to other political parties contesting the next general election.
item.content:encoded:
THERE are capable leaders within the Peoples Alliance party, says Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica.

In an interview on The Fiji Times online portal The Lens@177, Mr Kamikamica said this was one of the party’s strengths compared to other political parties contesting the next general election.

“One of the things that I started talking about which hopefully people can understand is when you look at People’s Alliance, it’s not just one individual,” he said.

“There are a lot of individuals that are leaders in their own right.

“(Ro Filipe) Tuisawau, (Filimoni) Vosarogo, (Sakiasi) Ditoka, (Lynda) Tabuya and then you got other assistant ministers like (Sakiusa) Tubuna and several others who are very capable people.

He said a number of current and new political parties relied heavily on one individual.

“Some of these parties are talking about one individual that is going to save Fiji.

“No one on their own can save this country.

“This country will only be saved if everybody works together.”

He added their collective experience, and common national goals set the party apart from others.

“There are parties in existence or are coming that have a broad bench strength with proven experience and they haven’t just come in to make money in politics.

“That is where I think Peoples Alliance sets itself apart from some of the other parties.”

item.title: BACK IN HISTORY | Weather tech boost
item.description: Fiji’s Meteorological Service received an $80,000 electrolytic hydrogen generator from American aid to produce gas for weather balloons at Nadi Airport. The Fiji Times reported on Monday, May 12, 1986, that the machine was the first of its kind in Fiji. It came with a back-up electricity generator worth about $5000.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji’s Meteorological Service received an $80,000 electrolytic hydrogen generator from American aid to produce gas for weather balloons at Nadi Airport.

The Fiji Times reported on Monday, May 12, 1986, that the machine was the first of its kind in Fiji. It came with a back-up electricity generator worth about $5000.

Ram Krishna, the Director of Meteorological Services then, explained how the generator worked.

“The electrolytic generator produced hydrogen by splitting water molecules through the use of electricity,” he said.

He said the new machine would save money and improve reliability.

“In the past, we used hydrogen imported from Australia at considerable expense. With the installation of the generator, the hydrogen was produced much more cheaply and provided greater reliability.”

The machine was put into operation at the Nadi Airport Weather Office that week. The aid was provided through the WMO (World Meteorological Organisation) Voluntary Assistance Programme.

The generator reduced costs and improved self-reliance for Fiji’s weather service, reflecting how international cooperation was helping to modernize technical services in the region during the 1980s.
